title: 2/2 Large-scale, single-cell characterization of molecular and cellular networks of mood regulation circuitry in major depressive disorder
text: The proposed study in an unprecedentedly large sample will significantly advance our understanding of the cellular and molecular pathways, and cell-specific transcriptomic profiles contributing to the neurobiological basis of major depressive disorder (MDD). Such a large sample of well-characterized postmortem brain tissue can only be achieved through a collaboration with a foreign site, bringing benefits to the US population through advances in our understanding and treatment of MDD. Through a better understanding of the mechanisms of depressive illness, we may be one step closer to developing novel treatment strategies and personalize interventions.

title: Papillomavirus pathogenesis and treatment in WHIM syndrome
text:
This research proposal will elucidate mechanisms of how WHIM mutation contributes to papillomavirus
pathogenesis, focusing on trafficking regulation of immune cells and viral life cycle regulation in keratinocytes.
Our studies are aimed at defining new therapeutic approaches to cure papillomavirus infections in WHIM
syndrome. These studies are highly relevant to public health because papillomavirus-associated malignancy is
a significant cause of mortality in WHIM syndrome.

title: Computational Method Development for 3D Spatial-Omics to Uncover Cellular Dynamics in Human Intestinal Aging
text:
Age-related changes in the human intestine, especially in immune system regulation, remain poorly understood
due to limitations in 2D imaging technology and incomplete molecular profiling. This research aims to create the
first comprehensive 3D atlas of the aging human intestine, integrating advanced imaging and computational tools
to map both the structural and molecular changes that occur with age. By unlocking new insights into how the
immune system ages in the intestine, this project could pave the way for broader applications in understanding
aging across other tissues and organs.

title: Selective targeting of TAF1 function in acute myeloid leukemia
text:
Dysregulated gene transcription is a major contributing factor in cancer, but the development of drugs interfering
with general transcription remains a challenging task. The protein TAF1 is a component of the transcription
machinery in eukaryotes, and TAF1 is a potential therapeutic target for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This
project aims at the development of first-in-class TAF1 targeting drugs for AML and other cancers that depend
on TAF1 functionality for survival and proliferation.

title: Cellular Imaging Core (CIC)
text: The Cellular Imaging Core (CIC) plays a pivotal role in the multidisciplinary research pipeline of IDDRC investigators at Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School. Located within the Kirby Neurobiology Center of Boston Children’s Hospital, this shared microscopy facility offers researchers access to high-end and specialized microscopy and digital imaging approaches which they can harness to understand the underlying mechanisms and structural changes associated with neurodevelopmental disorders. The Core offers widefield, confocal (multiphoton, laser-scanning, spinning disk) and super-resolution (stimulated emission depletion, STED) microscopes for high resolution subcellular localization of proteins of interest, for tracking live cells over prolonged periods of time, and for monitoring populations of cells in vivo in an awake, behaving animal. These instruments are accompanied with access to image analysis workstations, and importantly, to an extensive educational program that trains researchers one-on-one on the capabilities and limitations of each instrument and software package used. Core staff can also collaborate closely with IDDRC researchers in core-assisted projects to design, optimize and implement custom designed experiments or analysis approaches. Additionally, the Core offers Instrumentation and Technology Courses to inform the scientific community about what is new for state-of-the-art microscopy, to provide interactive, hands-on workshops on image acquisition, analysis and processing and to address issues in robustness with these imaging methods. Through these interactions with researchers, the Core identifies and obtains new equipment and technology that is relevant to our researchers. Taken together, here the CIC proposes a comprehensive program of collaboration with IDDRC investigators and other IDDRC Cores to lower the barrier for laboratories to incorporate novel and transformative microscopy technologies that elevate and accelerate our understanding of normal and pathological neural development, plasticity and function.

title: Core 2: Multi-omics Core
text: Summary Multi-Omics Core The Multi-Omics Core (MOC) is designed to generate comprehensive molecular data supporting the two project and overarching goals of the TARGET-AD consortium. By integrating genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics/lipidomics, and single-nucleus/cell RNA sequencing (penta-omics), the core will provide harmonized datasets from human brain tissue, matched blood, and iPSC-derived cultures to identify and validate Alzheimer’s disease (AD) subtypes and their candidate therapeutic targets. The MOC is structured around three primary aims. Aim 1 focuses on generating penta-omic data from well-characterized human cohorts (ROSMAP and MCSA), enabling the identification of molecular subtypes across matched brain and antemortem blood samples. Aim 2 extends this approach to iPSC-derived models, where omics profiling will be conducted following chemical and genetic target perturbations using AD-informer set compounds, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), and CRISPR genome editing. Aim 3 employs high-dimensional spatial profiling (Xenium and 4i imaging) to map subtype-specific molecular targets within brain tissue, providing critical insight into disease mechanisms and cell-type expression. To achieve these aims, the MOC utilizes cutting-edge mass spectrometry for proteomics and metabolomics, as well as advanced sequencing and imaging platforms for high-throughput, high- resolution multi-omics data generation. The innovative Alamar NuLISA platform will be used to measure established AD biomarkers (e.g., pTau and Aβ species) from its CNS panel in matched blood and iPSC-derived cell media, enabling the identification of peripheral signatures linked to brain subtypes. Harmonized protocols will be implemented to minimize batch effects and optimize data reproducibility. Importantly, the MOC will work in close collaboration with the Data Analytics Core (DAC), Experimental Modeling Core (EMC), and Admin and Data Management Core (ADMC) to ensure seamless data integration and dissemination. By providing open- access, rigorously annotated datasets, the MOC aims to facilitate the discovery of candidate subtype-specific therapeutic targets, advancing AD precision medicine initiatives.

title: Novel models to study dorsal root ganglion neurons in knee osteoarthritis pain
text:
Knee osteoarthritis is a primary cause of disability and chronic pain, with less than optimal first-line treatments
that are often invasive and inaccessible to patients—leading to an overreliance on analgesics like opioids,
which are dangerous, addictive, and ineffective with long-term use. The high burden of knee osteoarthritis-
induced pain warrants the need to develop novel analgesic strategies. This proposal combines cutting-edge
basic science techniques with clinically relevant models of knee osteoarthritis, to confront the problem of knee
osteoarthritis pain head-on and generate leads for future research into novel analgesics.

title: Lifespan Cellular and Spatial Mechanisms Linking Brain Aging and Alzheimer's Disease in the Human Prefrontal Cortex
text:
Age-related changes in the prefrontal cortex shape cognitive function and may increase vulnerability to
Alzheimer’s disease, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This proposal investigates how
lifespan-associated shifts in cellular trajectories, intercellular communication, and spatial organization
contribute to AD pathology. This work will provide a framework for developing targeted interventions to promote
cognitive resilience and prevent neurodegeneration.

title: Impact of Acid, Base, and Salt Components of E-cigarettes in Pregnancy
text:
The United States Surgeon General recently announced vaping of electronic cigarettes (e-cigs) as a major public
health concern. Utilizing a state-of-the-art custom-engineered vaping system with a commercial e-cig unit and
atomizer identical to those sold in vape shops world-wide, the proposed studies dissect the health effects of
acidic, basic, and salt components of e-cigs during pregnancy, test novel approaches in perinatal e-cig field, and
pave the way for strategic sex-dependent treatment design. The proposed studies develop a strong mechanistic
framework for e-cig-induced developmental adaptations and directly address several “Research Areas of
Emphasis” of NIEHS Strategic Plan 2025-2029.

title: 01 - Cancer Biology & Immunology
text: ABSTRACT – CANCER BIOLOGY AND IMMUNOLOGY (CBI) PROGRAM Overview and Goals: The goals of the Cancer Biology and Immunology (CBI) program are to identify basic mechanisms of cancer cell biology and the immune response in order to develop novel therapeutic approaches to treat cancer. In particular, CBI members are interested in the transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms controlling tumor and immune cell function, the impact of metabolism and metabolites on tumor and immune cell biology, and the role of the microenvironment in tumor biology and immune activity. Research Highlights: CBI investigators recently showed that the CXCL12/CXCR4 axis is an important target in both Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) and Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML). Targeting CXCR4 on AML promotes oxidative stress and terminal differentiation of leukemic stem cells (Cell Rep. 20201), whereas blockade of CXCL12 combined with tyrosine kinase inhibitors eliminates CML stem cells (Cell Stem Cell 20192). CBI investigators also defined how metabolites influence tumor and immune cell activities: tumor-derived L-2-hydroxyglutarate influences renal cancer progression and prognosis (Clin. Cancer Res. 20183), and alpha-ketoglutarate regulates the differentiation and function of CD4 T cells (Immunity 20174). Mechanistic discoveries by CBI investigators have led to therapeutics that are now being tested in clinical trials, including a heparanase inhibitor for multiple myeloma (Haematologica 20185) and a DNMT1 inhibitor for MDS and AML (NCT04167917). Program Activities: CBI catalyzes intra- and inter-programmatic interactions via monthly meetings, annual retreats, and seminars. Technology forums introduce members to new and existing capabilities of the Shared Resources, and members' discoveries are advanced from the bench to Phase I clinical trials through pilot funding from the Alabama Drug Discovery Alliance and the O'Neal Invests program. Members: CBI has 57 members from 16 Departments/Divisions who have a combined $5.2M in NCI funding and $10.1M in total cancer-relevant, peer- reviewed grants. In the current cycle, CBI members published 693 cancer-relevant publications, of which 39% were inter-programmatic and 23% were intra-programmatic collaborations and 18% of which are in journals with impact factor of 9 or greater. Future Directions: In line with the O'Neal strategic plan, CBI will focus on the role of obesity and metabolism in regulating cancer progression and the anti-tumor immune response. Of the 13 cancers linked with obesity, CBI investigators already have strength in tumor biology and anti-tumor immunity in multiple myeloma, renal, breast, and ovarian cancers, and we expect that these efforts will lead to collaborative, multi-PI grants in the next funding period. These cancers overlap with those being targeted by our Community Outreach and Engagement office, in part due to their relevance to the catchment area. Finally, CBI members will leverage imaging techniques developed by ET to follow tumor cell activity and immune cell reactivity in situ.

title: SPORE in Prostate Cancer
text:
Overall Project Narrative
This SPORE is dedicated to improving outcomes from prostate cancer, which affects 1 in 8 men in the United
States, by delivering three new approaches to prostate cancer treatment. Over the planned 5 years of funding,
three new combinatorial treatment strategies will be evaluated in clinical trials and in correlative laboratory-based
studies to assess their effectiveness in men with prostate cancer.

title: Plasma Cells in Health and Disease
text:
Antibody-Secreting Cells (ASC), including Plasma Cells, are the cells responsible for the
production of protective antibodies in response to infections and vaccinations. However, rogue
ASC that produce undesired antibodies against human tissues are also responsible for myriad
antibody-mediated diseases including autoimmune diseases, allergy and transplant rejection. In
this project, we will study the different types of ASC that provide protection and induce disease to
understand their nature and regulatory programs. The information gained will improve our ability
to design safer and more effective treatments multiple antibody-mediated diseases and
modulatory strategies to optimize protective vaccine responses.

title: Understanding Available Resources and Delivery of Recovery Services in a College Setting
text:
Campus recovery communities are a place where students can be engaged in their recovery and supported by
the colleges and universities they attend. Our study will collect data from 30 colleges and universities to detail
what resources and treatments are available to students for recovery support, as well as recruit 30 students
from each site (900 total) to assess the utilization of the available resources at their collegiate setting. Findings
from this research will be used to inform the development of a cell-phone-based alcohol prevention
intervention with social network and location-based recovery support tools for adults in recovery for alcohol-
related problems.

title: The role of VAMP2 in alpha-synuclein function and pathology
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because alpha-synuclein pathology is linked to various
neurological diseases including Parkinson’s disease and Lewy body dementia, and understanding the
underlying disease mechanisms will allow us to develop a novel intervention therapy. Thus, this research is
relevant to the NIH’s mission that pertains to supporting the ongoing basic research, foster research that has
immediate medical relevance, and encourage translational research that links the discoveries from basic
research into therapeutic interventions for treating neurological disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and
Lewy body dementia.

title: Alcohol-induced neuromodulation of sleep-wake circuits: Insights from Drosophila
text:
Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a major public health problem that causes millions of deaths each year and is
strongly associated with persistent sleep and circadian disturbances that increase relapse risk. This project will
investigate how alcohol alters the release of the neuropeptide PDF from specific brain circuits in Drosophila
and how these signals shape tolerance and sleep disruption. By revealing conserved mechanisms of alcohol-
induced neuroadaptation, the findings will inform strategies to stabilize sleep and reduce relapse in individuals
with AUD.

title: Understanding the regulation of mtDNA heteroplasmy and integrity
text:
Mutations in the mitochondrial genome play an important role in a number of devastating maternally inherited
diseases, as well as a number of human relevant pathologies, including cancer, sarcopenia, and neurodegener-
ation, but the cellular mechanisms that give rise to them or modify their presence are poorly understood. This
project is designed to take advantage of cutting edge technologies to test fundamental hypotheses involving what
cellular mechanisms modify their presence. The end result will be a better understanding of mitochondrial biology
and the role of mitochondrial mutation in human diseases.

title: Low-Profile 3D-Printed Radiopaque Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds
text:
Polymeric bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVSs) have emerged as a potential solution to problems
with traditional metal stents by providing initial support to prevent recoil and slowly degrading to restore
vasomotion and eliminate residual foreign materials that may contribute to restenosis. However, currently
approved BVS have higher incidences of major cardiovascular events and clotting in small arteries due to their
strut size and slow, pro-inflammatory degrading polymer. We will develop and test in vivo 3D-printed, low
profile, drug-eluting, biocompatible and mechanically functional BVS.

title: In Vitro Diagnostic for Fungal Pathogens
text: To support the development of promising diagnostics technologies for emerging and reemerging infectious diseases. Areas of support may focus on improving performance of agnostic nucleic acid sequencing solutions on commercial platforms; methods that improve protein analyte detection; and efforts to improve direct-from-blood or other biofluid detection and identification of microbial infection.

title: Molecular mechanisms of mechanosensation in the cardiac pacemaker
text:
The heart is one of the most mechanically dynamic organs; it dilates and contracts to cycle its volume in order
to pump between 5 to 30 liters of blood a minute. Heart stretch accelerates heart rate; however, how the
pacemaker cells controlling heart rate sense and respond to mechanical stretch is unknown. We aim to identify
the molecules behind mechanosensation in the cardiac pacemaker.

title: Aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling in Airway Inflammation
text:
Asthma is characterized by chronic inflammation and airway thickening in the conducting airways
leading to respiratory symptoms, lung function decline, and exacerbation. Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is
an important modulator of host-environment interactions and inflammation, suggesting it may have a key role
in asthma pathogenesis. We propose that activation of the AhR signaling in airway smooth muscle (ASM) will
reduce inflammation-induced airway hyperresponsiveness and remodeling in asthma. Our studies using
human ASM from both non-asthmatics vs. asthmatics, along with animal studies, where we knockout AhR in
smooth muscle, will substantially enhance our understanding of how AhR in ASM influence the asthmatic
airway structure and function. This is a clinically important step to gain basic fundamental knowledge in the
development of novel therapeutic strategies to mitigate remodeling aspects of asthma.
